abstract: Canonical green fluorescent proteins typically regulate chromophore photophysics through a rigid beta-barrel environment, while spectral tuning often relies on protein engineering or directed evolution. Here, we design a compact alpha-helical protein pocket that activates a GFP-chromophore-derived fluorogen and accommodates a series of chemically modified ligands. A co-crystal structure reveals shared anchoring interactions for fluorogen activation and contacts that enable ligand-dependent spectral tuning. Guided by this structure, ligand substitution shifts emission across the red-to-green range while retaining the same protein scaffold. Quantitative binding and photophysical analyses establish the structural and chemical determinants of affinity, fluorescence activation, and spectral tuning, and the resulting fluorogens function in living cells. Finally, structure-guided substitutions repurpose the pocket toward a distinct drug ligand. These results establish an alpha-helical route to programmable fluorogen activation in which optical properties can be tuned through ligand design rather than repeated protein evolution.
